section_name: Introduction: Two Components of Writing Instruction
content:
Episode 1 K-12 — Introduction: Two Components of Writing Instruction

Hello, I'm Kristina Smekens. And in this 20-min video, I'll address the two major components needed to teach writing.

Learning to write well, like anything else, requires both instruction and practice. The learner needs expert instruction from someone who is knowledgeable on the skill, and the learner needs extensive practice in order to perfect the skill himself.

Therefore, just assigning writing isn't enough to improve writer abilities. We have to spend time teaching students how to execute grade level writing skills. We need to actively and deliberately teach students specific techniques to master persuasive, informative, and narrative writing at their grade levels.

Episode 1 K-12 — Component 1: Explicit Instruction via Mini-Lessons

During Tier 1, whole-class instruction, teachers are to introduce one writing skill at a time. These lessons clearly explain what the skill is, why it's important, when and where to use it, and most importantly, how to execute it in writing. Each skill is taught through step-by-step explanations, revealed within strong writing examples, and made transparent through teacher think-alouds and demonstrations.

Now it's important to distinguish these skill-based writing lessons from all of the other writing activities that we provide throughout the school day. Since anything and everything could be labeled as "a lesson" of some kind, this particular type of instruction is commonly referred to as a "mini-lesson."

A mini lesson teaches the how of a grade-level writing skill, and it is mini in that it's delivered within 15 minutes or less.

Now, there is a lot more to planning and delivering a writing mini-lesson, and I'll address that in a separate video, but for now, just know that before we can assign writing tasks, we have to teach writing skills.

section_name: Component 2: Daily Writing Practice After Mini-Lessons
content:
Episode 1 K-12 — Component 2: Daily Writing Practice After Mini-Lessons

The second component necessary to improve writers is to provide them with plenty of opportunities to attempt the new skills they have learned.

Watching and listening to the teacher demonstrate a writing technique is incredibly helpful. It gives students a clear model to follow. However, what students often don't realize is the complex thinking and decision-making that goes into it. Everything sounds good when the teacher says it. Everything looks easy when the teacher does it.

However, the process of applying a new skill to one's own writing is a complicated journey filled with choices and challenges. Therefore, students need ample time to tackle and grapple with these skills. Mastery doesn't happen just by listening to a teacher talk about it. No one "gets good" at something by watching someone else do it. That's why it's crucial to allocate time for students to write immediately after each mini-lesson. This is when the "work" in writer's workshop truly begins.

While kids try out the new skill during writing time, the teacher is looking over shoulders and reading off of screens. And this is when it becomes clear what students understand and misunderstand. What seemed simple and straightforward during the lesson is much more difficult when students try to put it into practice. But this makes sense -- when learning something new, it's natural to make mistakes and encounter challenges. This is why every mini-lesson should be followed with additional time for students to write in class. When attempting anything the first couple of times, the learner needs the expert to be nearby. In the case of writing, this is when the teacher guides, reminds, clarifies, and encourages.

Episode 1 K-12 — Making Time for Writing Instruction

Now, some teachers have a class period or section that is completely devoted to writing instruction and practice. Some elementary teachers have a block of time on their daily schedule labeled "Writing." It is posted as a regular subject and gets the same attention as math, reading, recess, and lunch.

However, too often writing does not have its own carved-out time slot. In fact, there is a lot of educational research that details teacher "confessions" that they would do more writing if only they had more time.

Well, I don't have a magic schedule to offer you in this video. And I don't think you will just "find" time to teach writing in your already-packed school day.

What I believe it will take is choosing to make the time. We have to make time for regular writing instruction and in-class writing experiences. We can't improve student writing without it.

Now, making time will require us to study our schedules, tighten our transitions between activities, and massage the minutes that we do have.

I know it's easy for me to say and much harder to do. So let's look at some practical ways to achieve this. And while I share some scheduling ideas, recognize that there is not a one-size-fits-all solution. Every classroom is different. So, while I'll offer some possibilities, I encourage you to be open minded, to consider elements and nuances of the scheduling ideas that are applicable.

After sharing some options, I'll conclude this video with next steps related to your specific situation.

section_name: Elementary Scheduling: Anchoring Writing to Content Areas
content:
Episode 1 K-12 — Elementary Scheduling: Anchoring Writing to Content Areas

OK, let me start with the self-contained elementary teacher who is juggling all subjects. Again, finding another 30 min for "writing" is nearly impossible.

So let's look at it another way. Consider the writer's workshop as a flexible facet that is anchored to other subjects throughout the day.

Deliver subject-area instruction as usual. This may include reading from textbooks, leading discussions, and more. After sharing the new content, it's common to ask students to write about it. However, before they begin, provide a 10 min mini lesson targeting a relevant writing skill.

For example, after you've delivered some information on a content-area concept like the water cycle or the American Revolution, prepare to give students a short writing task related to what they just learned. This could be anything from writing a clear explanation to developing a single persuasive reason.

Now, before announcing the task, conduct a mini-lesson focused on a specific skill that would impact the type of writing you will assign. Then, transition into "workshop" mode where students write about content-area concept, applying the new writing skill.

Remember, you already set aside time for teaching the subject matter and having kids write about it. The only addition is to insert a 10-min mini lesson about an informative, persuasive, or narrative writing skill. Remember, just assigning writing in the content areas isn't enough. We have to spend time teaching students how to execute grade level writing skills -- otherwise they are only practicing what they already know how to do, or worse, generating more weak writing for us to grade.

Take note that this approach is not replacing subject area or content standards -- in fact we're enhancing them, because scientists summarize ideas and share findings. Historians interpret events and argue perspectives. Even mathematicians explain their problem-solving process and justify their thinking.

By weaving in relevant writing skills alongside subject matter, students have content and information to write about. This transforms their knowledge from isolated facts to a deeper understanding of the concepts.

What I love about this scheduling approach is that it eliminates the need to find a whole separate time slot for writing. Now the mini-lesson and writing time are seamlessly connected to a content area.

In fact, look to anchor the writing mini lesson to a different subject area each week. This reiterates that scientists, historians, and mathematicians write.

Hey, here is one more benefit -- these writing experiences provide two potential grades. They can be assessed for content accuracy and students' writing skills.

section_name: Primary Teachers: Two Daily Writing Lessons
content:
Episode 1 K-12 — Primary Teachers: Two Daily Writing Lessons

OK, this first scheduling option is applicable for writing in the content areas. Now I want to provide a clarification for primary teachers and those who work with English learners and students with special needs.

I have no doubt you are teaching writing daily. I'm positive you are targeting concepts of print, handwriting, letter formation, directionality, and sentence conventions. And as imperative as these are, they all fall under language foundations. This is one of two daily writing lessons young writers need.

Young writers also need to learn how to express their own opinions in persuasives, how to demonstrate their individual knowledge in informatives, and how to share personal stories in narratives.

While students are learning sentence conventions, they must also be learning how to express their own ideas in pictures, letter labels, and simple words. It's not first teach language foundations and then how to express their ideas. It's two separate lessons serving two different purposes that are taught parallel to one another all year long.

Compare this to teaching reading. All year you provide instruction-and-practice on decoding and instruction-and-practice on comprehension. The goal is that when the decoding principles click, students aren't just word callers, but actually understand what they're reading.

This is how it works for writing, too. As students learn more about the concepts of print and sentence conventions, they begin to apply them to their own persuasive, informative, and narrative writing topics.

My point is that it's crucial to have two separate time slots in the daily schedule for teaching writing in the primary grades -- one for language foundations and second for expressing ideas in developmental writing stages.

section_name: Secondary Scheduling: Balancing Reading and Writing
content:
Episode 1 K-12 — Secondary Scheduling: Balancing Reading and Writing

Alright, I've described scheduling considerations for elementary teachers, now let's look at the realities of the departmentalized language arts teacher who is responsible for teaching both reading and writing.

"Getting it all in" within a traditional 50-minute period can be a serious juggling act.

And for veteran teachers who have tried to cram reading and writing into the same daily class period, it's often a nightmare. Picture it -- You start class with a 10-15 min comprehension mini lesson and then transition to reading time. After opening a text and recapping where you left off, you get through only a page or two and it's time to switch to writing. After delivering a writing mini lesson, students compose a couple sentences just before the bell rings.

Although it is ideal to instruct on reading and writing every single day, accomplishing this within a traditional language arts class period often causes more teacher frustration than skill improvement. There never seems to be any time spent digging into reading or writing. The students barely get started, and they have to stop.

To resolve this, some middle school and high school language arts teachers opt for a schedule of reading for several weeks and then writing for several weeks. Although this may feel less hectic, there is a harsh reality. This pendulum swing creates long writing lulls that are weeks apart, making "use it or lose it" a constant struggle. After teaching anything, if the learner doesn't apply the skill regularly, he quickly forgets how to do it.

So, rather than focusing on reading or writing for weeks at a time, consider a class schedule that highlights reading and writing to occur every week. This allows for immersion in one subject for the entire period, but not for the entire month.

Episode 1 K-12 — Secondary Weekly Schedule Options

When planning this on paper, it seems logical to target reading and writing every other day.

But teachers often realize that they have to start every class by reviewing where they left off two days earlier. We can shorten the space between reading and writing days if we execute some of them consecutively. This often leads to teaching and practicing reading comprehension on Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday and teaching and practicing writing on Thursday and Friday.

Now, that is definitely a possibility. But let me propose another option. This accounts for some consecutive days for reading and writing, but another plus is that the teacher can now bridge the weekend, connecting the instruction from the last class meeting on Friday with the next class meeting on Monday. Compare this to the previous option that created an undesirable 5-day gap before returning to it.

Since a school week includes 5 days, I give reading comprehension more time in first semester and writing the majority during second semester. So the final schedule might look like this:

First semester, I teach and practice reading comprehension on Mondays, Tuesdays, and Fridays, with writing mini lessons and writing time on Wednesdays and Thursdays.

Then I adjust the schedule for second semester, offering three days for writing and two days for reading.

Episode 1 K-12 — Block Schedule: Major-Minor Workshop Approach

Let me offer one more version for the secondary language arts teacher -- this one for those working within a 70-80-or-90 min block schedule.

The extended time of a block schedule offers a golden opportunity to nurture both reading and writing every day.

Initially many teachers split the time evenly between reading and writing. But another possibility is to emphasize one workshop more than the other each day. This immersion helps grow stamina so that writers can compose longer texts and readers can comprehend multiple sources, all in one sitting.

On Monday, Tuesday, and Friday, Reader's workshop takes center stage. After comprehension mini lesson, dive into texts, fostering analysis, discussion, and independent reading for the next 35 min.

Then, on Thursday and Friday, Writer's workshop takes the lead. After a 10-min mini lesson, students focus on applying the writing skill within a 35 min independent writing time.

This leaves 25 minutes to be dedicated to the opposite workshop every day. This includes a short mini-lesson and quick reading or writing experience.

Applying the principles of the major-minor workshop allows for intense work and deep dives in each area while ensuring regular touch points for the other, keeping all skills fresh.

Now, there is an exception to this major and minor workshop approach. If your block is set up with A and B schedules -- meaning that you don't see all of your students every day, then execute a more even split of reading and writing each day.

Episode 1 K-12 — Key Takeaways and Next Steps

I've now shared several ways to make time for writing, to routinely provide a writing mini lesson followed by a chance for students to practice the skill in class.

As I wrap up this video, let me identify the most important takeaways. Teaching writing requires that we:

- Teach grade-level writing skills via 10-15 min mini lessons.
- Follow every mini lesson with an opportunity for students to try the skill in our presence.
- And that this instruction and practice combination occurs regularly throughout the school week.

So if those are the key takeaways, let's look to your next steps.

I encourage you to assess the frequency that writing instruction and practice are currently happening.

Review your schedule and discuss ways you might be able to massage your minutes. Specifically look for opportunities to:

- Transition between classroom activities more quickly.
- Combine or rotate every day activities.
- And/or streamline management and procedures to regain some minutes.

All of this will help you take the next step toward building better writers.
